title: Human 1.0: Water:Fat in the breast
text:
Summary


Human 1.0 shows that the difference between NORMAL and CANCER breasts is in the water-rich scans. Measured there, a basic analysis points to the CANCER breast rather than the NORMAL one, matching synchrotron and ex-vivo data on the water-rich side.


What we expect: a normal breast is mostly fat with some glandular/fibrous tissue. Cancer replaces fat with cells and remodelled fibrous tissue, which hold more water. Each breast gets one number, its Water:Fat ratio: the area of its water peak divided by the area of its fat peak, from two fitted Gaussians. Comparing a patient’s two breasts, the CANCER breast should have the higher Water:Fat.


Data: 258 patients analysed with Human 1.0 (NORMAL, BENIGN or CANCER); 251 used, after leaving out 7 with a large left/right intensity imbalance (Appendix I).



1. The difference is in the water-rich scans
In the fattiest 15% of samples the three cohorts look the same; in the wettest 15% they separate NORMAL < BENIGN < CANCER. The information is in the water-rich tissue — denser breasts are better for us; mammography’s weakness is our strength (Chapter 1).


2. It matches other data
That wettest-15% ordering matches synchrotron and Keele ex-vivo data. A fixed water-peak threshold for single-point scans (Appendix C) also keeps the wet tissue; the paired test there supports CANCER vs NORMAL (Chapter 2).


3. Rigorous tumour targeting is not needed
The tumours are small and only a few beams are placed approximately, yet the signal holds where the beam goes through glandular tissue: changes appear wide-reaching in the glandular breast, not confined to the tumour (Chapter 3).


4. Mapping for Human 2.0 Proposal
Scan a grid over the whole breast and select the wettest tissue after the scan. The water-peak rule (Appendix C) could be a stopgap on Human 1.0; mapping is the recommendation (Chapter 4).

A pilot result: 18 CANCER/NORMAL patients, 95% CI 59%–96%, and mostly dense breasts. All limitations are in Chapter 5.

title: 1  The difference between cohorts is in the water-rich scans

NoteFinding 1



In the fattiest 15% of samples the three cohorts look the same. In the wettest 15% they separate: NORMAL 0.81 < BENIGN 0.96 < CANCER 1.07 (water peak height). The information is in the water-rich tissue.


Every prepared sample from Nova 250 onwards (intensity-imbalanced patients left out) is shown in Figure 1.1: by Nova number, and ordered by water peak height (the mean of the prepared curve over q = 20-22; preparation sets the fat peak to 1, Appendix A). The wettest and fattiest 15% are marked.
Figure 1.2 averages those two bands by cohort. The fattiest 15% overlaps for all three labels (water peak about 0.12). The wettest 15% pulls apart. Most breast cancers arise in the glandular tissue [1] [3], and tumours remodel the fibrous tissue around them [5], so a scan through fat sees little of it.
Denser is better for us. Dense breasts hold more glandular, water-rich tissue — exactly where this signal lives. That is where mammography is weakest (density can hide masses) [8] [9], so mammography’s weakness is our strength: the same tissue that hurts X-ray contrast is what XRD needs. For mapping, keep the wettest points after a whole-breast scan (e.g. the top 15% within each breast) and compare those (Chapter 4).

title: 2  Our data match synchrotron and ex-vivo data
text:
2.2 Keele ex-vivo data
Figure 2.2 shows ex-vivo scans of breast tissue measured at Keele University [13], one heatmap each for Healthy, Benign and grade 3 cancer tissue, each row one normalised scan.
The water peak is missing from these scans: they stop at q ≈ 17 nm⁻¹, below the water peak at q ≈ 20-22, so we cannot see the water rise directly. The reduction in the fat peak, however, is clear: in the Healthy tissue a large share of the scans are dominated by a bright fat peak at q ≈ 14, in Benign it covers fewer, and in the grade 3 cancer it covers a smaller share still. Less fat is the other side of the same change that our water-rich scans and the synchrotron data show as a higher water peak.






Figure 2.2: Ex-vivo XRD scans of breast tissue measured at Keele, normalised, one heatmap per cohort: Healthy, Benign and grade 3 cancer. The scans stop at q ≈ 17 nm⁻¹, so the water peak is not measured, but the fat peak at q ≈ 14 clearly weakens towards cancer.

Figure 3.1: Tumour size of every CANCER breast with a reported size. Left: linear extent in the biopsy cores (pathology). Right: largest mass on imaging (mammogram, ultrasound or MRI). Blue: breast has at least one usable, water-rich scan; grey: only rejected (fatty) scans. One dot per breast.
Over every CANCER breast with a reported size, the tumours run from 2 to 18 mm on biopsy (median 9 mm, 62 breasts) and from 5 to 95 mm on imaging (median 20 mm, 69 breasts). Usable and rejected-only breasts have similar size ranges (imaging medians 20 mm and 18 mm), so having a water-rich scan is not simply a matter of a larger tumour. The biopsy size is only the length of tumour along a needle core; imaging measures the mass itself and is the better sense of how large a target the tumour is. Even so, most are a couple of centimetres or less. Size by grade is in Appendix H.
Each breast is scanned only a few times — typically 3 beams — and the operator places them from a quadrant, a clock position and a distance from the nipple. The breast sits differently on our instrument than on the mammogram. Hitting a 20 mm mass with 3 approximately placed beams is unlikely to be the rule; missing the tumour altogether will often be the case. We have no data on where each beam landed relative to the tumour, so this is an argument from the sizes and the scanning practice, not a measured miss rate.

title: 3  Rigorous targeting of the tumour is not necessary
text:
3.2 Yet the glandular signal holds
What we do measure is whether each beam went through water-rich, glandular tissue (Chapter 1, Appendix C). When both breasts have at least one such scan, the CANCER breast is the wetter one in most CANCER/NORMAL patients, across the size range of Figure 3.1. Fatty scans of the same breasts do not carry the signal. So the result does not require the tumour in the beam; it requires glandular tissue.
A working hypothesis is that the cancer changes tissue beyond the tumour itself — a sphere of influence — and that those changes are expressed in the glandular/fibrous tissue of the breast. Tumours remodel the fibrous stroma around them [5], and X-ray scattering has detected structural changes in and next to breast tumours [6] [7]. How far that region reaches cannot be measured from these data. What the data support is the practical claim: high positioning accuracy on the tumour is not needed; what matters is that each scan reaches glandular tissue.

title: 4  A proposal for Human 2.0: mapping the breast
text:
4.1 A Human 1.0 stopgap: the water-peak filter during scanning
The water-peak rule of Appendix C could be applied while the patient is on the instrument. At each position it needs a short scan, long enough to see the fat and water peaks; a quick analysis of that scan (correct the peak position, normalise, and check the water peak height against 0.35 with the water centred at q ≥ 19); and a decision: if the scan is water-rich the full scan proceeds, and if not the operator moves to a clearly different spot. The scanning software would need this analysis built in, much like the existing transmission check (Phase 1) that decides whether a position is scanned. In theory, this could be implemented on Human 1.0. It still depends on where the operator puts the beam, and gives a few points per breast.

title: 4  A proposal for Human 2.0: mapping the breast
text:
4.2 The recommendation: mapping
To map the breast is to scan a grid of points, each for a short time, and decide afterwards which points to use. Each point gives a full 1D curve I(q), so a map is a 3D matrix: two positions (x, y) and q. Each point holds a curve, and each q holds an image of the breast at that q. Figure 4.1 shows an example measured at Ulster University on a tissue sample: a 26 × 25 grid at 0.5 mm spacing, 1 s per point, with 336 points measured and 210 of them on the tissue sample. The rest see only the empty holder. No background is subtracted.


Code
extent = (x_mm[0] - 0.25, x_mm[-1] + 0.25, y_mm[0] - 0.25, y_mm[-1] + 0.25)
panels = (("Total intensity", np.where(measured, total, np.nan), "viridis"),
          ("Fat band, q 13-15", np.where(on_sample, band(cube, MAP_FAT), np.nan), "viridis"),
          ("Water band, q 19.5-22.5", np.where(on_sample, band(cube, MAP_WATER), np.nan), "viridis"),
          ("Water / fat (3 × 3 mean)", ratio_3, "coolwarm"))
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(8, 2.6))
for ax, (title, image, colours) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.set_facecolor("white")
    ax.imshow(np.where(measured & ~on_sample, 1, np.nan), origin="lower", extent=extent, cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=4)
    low, high = np.nanpercentile(image, (2, 98))

    fig.colorbar(shown, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.03)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="x (mm)")
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)

plt.show()
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10








Figure 4.1: The Ulster map, one value per point. Left to right: the total scattered intensity (the sample against the empty holder), the fat band (q 13-15), the water band (q 19.5-22.5), and the water band over the fat band, with each point averaged with its neighbours (3 × 3). Grey points are off the sample; white points were not measured.





Mapping works much like an XRD video rather than a snapshot. At every point we gather a frame. Each frame on its own has a low XRD signal-to-noise ratio, but it can be used as it is for transmission, giving high spatial resolution. Conversely, we can sum over more frames, covering more distance, for a better XRD signal-to-noise ratio at lower spatial resolution. The trade-off is chosen after the scan, and can be different for different questions.
A single 1 s point gives a noisy curve, but neighbouring points can be added together. Figure 4.2 shows one point in the middle of the sample on its own, and the mean of its 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 neighbourhoods and of every point on the sample: the fat and water peaks only become clear once points are added. On their own, the points are as noisy as the differences across the sample: neighbouring points differ in water/fat by about 0.10 from noise alone, while the 3 × 3 means range from 0.82 to 1.12 across the sample. Averaging n points cuts the noise by about √n, by 3 for a 3 × 3 block.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(curves), figsize=(8, 2.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, curve, n) in zip(axes, curves):

    ax.set(title=f"{name}\n({n} s of scanning)", xlabel="q (nm⁻¹)", xlim=Q_SHOWN)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10








Figure 4.2: Adding points improves the 1D curve. One point in the middle of the sample on its own, and the mean of its 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 neighbourhoods and of every point on the sample. The grey bands mark the fat and water bands.





Because every point is kept, the map can be used in two ways after the scan:

Select regions. Points can be grouped by what they show — in particular the wettest 15% within each breast (Figure 1.1, Figure 1.2) — and only those used for the breast’s Water:Fat. That is a percentile inside the breast, not a fixed threshold on a few single points. A fixed water-peak threshold can still drop empty or too-dry points first; the ranking then picks the best tissue that remains. Figure 4.3 splits the sample into its most fatty, middle and most water-rich thirds by the 3 × 3 water/fat: the mean curves differ clearly, the fattiest with a fat peak standing above the water and the most water-rich with the two about level.
Compare whole breasts. The distribution of water/fat over every point of one breast can be compared with that of the other breast, rather than a few single points. This uses the whole breast and does not depend on where the tumour is (Chapter 3).

Figure 4.3: Selecting regions after the scan. Left: the sample split into thirds by the 3 × 3 water/fat (fattiest, middle, most water-rich). Middle: the mean curve of each third. Right: the distribution of the 3 × 3 water/fat over every point of the sample, the kind of whole-breast summary that could be compared between a patient’s two breasts.





Mapping gives a whole-breast analysis: we can tell the adipose and glandular areas apart, analyse them separately if we want, and get an idea of where interesting tissue is — on the hypothesis of a tumour sphere of influence (Chapter 3) — without aiming at the tumour or deciding at the instrument.

title: 4  A proposal for Human 2.0: mapping the breast
section: 4.3 How long would a whole-breast map take?
text:
4.3 How long would a whole-breast map take?
The practical picture is a continuous fly-scan, not a stop-and-dwell grid. The detector runs at 1 Hz, and the source and detector move together at a preset speed. That speed sets how long the beam spends on each volume of the breast, and so how many photons each 1 s frame collects. Dose and XRD signal-to-noise both follow from that choice.
Surface scan first (radiation off). A very rapid initial pass, under 10 s, measures the thickness of the breast at each point with the beam off. That surface map does three jobs:

Choose where to scan. Regions below a thickness cut (for example thinner than 2 cm) can be left out, so time and dose go only where the breast is thick enough to be useful.
Support q corrections. Thickness (or distance) can be used to correct the curves if needed. The Water:Fat ratio analysis itself does not require a distance measurement.
Turn transmission into linear attenuation. With thickness known, transmission becomes a linear attenuation map — a measure of breast density — at high spatial resolution. That transmission map is valuable on its own, and it is also what later marks regions of interest for XRD analysis.

Then the XRD scan. Once the region of interest is set from the surface and transmission maps, a scan protocol is designed to keep the time down. Speed can be dynamic: slower over thicker tissue so enough photons are collected, faster where the breast is thinner. Neighbouring 1 Hz frames can still be summed afterwards for a cleaner XRD curve at the cost of spatial resolution (Figure 4.2); the transmission values keep the fine grid.
We expect these scans to take no longer than 5 minutes. Absolute dose in mGy has not been estimated here and has to be confirmed on the instrument.






NoteMapping is the recommendation for Human 2.0



Mapping gives a whole-breast analysis: noisy single points are summed into clean curves, and which regions to analyse is decided after the scan. The water-peak rule (Appendix C) is a possible stopgap on Human 1.0.

title: 5  Limitations
text:
WarningWhat limits these results




Small numbers. The headline rests on 18 CANCER/NORMAL patients: 83%, with a 95% confidence interval of 59%–96%. It is a pilot result.
Only CANCER vs NORMAL is supported on the threshold rule. The wettest 15% of samples separate NORMAL < BENIGN < CANCER (Figure 1.2), but under the fixed usable-scan cut of Appendix C BENIGN and CANCER look almost the same, and the paired test for BENIGN vs NORMAL is 10/27 (37%) and for CANCER vs BENIGN 2/5 (40%), neither above chance. Distinguishing benign from cancer is what clinicians need most, and this analysis does not yet do it. Mapping would address this: a whole-breast map lets us keep the wettest tissue in each breast (the top-15% idea of Chapter 1) and compare that, instead of a few single points that only just clear a fixed threshold (Chapter 4).
Few young CANCER breasts. Only 2 CANCER breasts under 40 have a usable scan, so nothing can be said about that age group (Section D.3).
A thin healthy baseline. Only 2 NORMAL/NORMAL patients have usable scans in both breasts, so how different two healthy breasts are is barely measured (Appendix D).
The rule selects dense breasts. BI-RADS C/D (dense) make up 82% of the patients compared against 39% of those left out (Figure D.6). The result applies to dense breasts; for fattier breasts it currently says nothing.
The threshold sits at a peak. The CANCER vs NORMAL share is 68% at 0.25 (17/25), 83% at 0.35 (15/18), 67% at 0.45 (10/15), 78% at 0.55 (7/9). The chosen 0.35 is at a peak of this curve (Figure D.1), so the 83% is likely the optimistic end, and it was chosen on the same patients it is reported on. The result stays above chance at every threshold. Mapping would address this: selection becomes a percentile within each breast after the scan, not a global threshold tuned on this cohort (Chapter 4).

title: Appendix A — Preparing each scan: peak-shift correction and min-max normalisation
text:
Three example scans, from Nova 250 onwards and one data batch, with a clear fat peak, chosen so their fat peaks start at different q; the red one also has a strong water peak near q = 21. The dots mark each fitted fat peak.

As measured: the fat peak’s position depends on the sample-to-detector distance (SDD), which differs a little between scans, so the peaks don’t line up.
Peak-shift corrected: a Gaussian plus a straight-line baseline is fitted to I(q) between q = 10 and 17.5 nm⁻¹, and the fat peak’s position is the Gaussian’s centre, so the baseline’s slope can’t move it. Each scan’s SDD is then changed (new SDD = SDD · tan 2θ(peak) / tan 2θ(14)), the image integrated again and the peak refitted, repeating until the fitted centre is at q = 14 nm⁻¹ (nova_sdd_peak_align.py). The thick lines in panels 1 and 2 are those fits, the dotted lines their baselines.
Min-max normalised (Stretch): each corrected curve is rescaled so its trough (the minimum of a cubic over q = 5-10) is 0 and the fit’s value at its peak is 1.

The first two panels are in measured units and the third is 0-1, so they share the q axis but not the y axis.


Code

WATER_EXAMPLE = (13.1, 0.8)         # a fourth scan with a strong water peak: measured fat peak nearest 13.1, stretched level over q 20-22 at least 0.8
Q_START = 1  # nm⁻¹, where every q axis starts
EXAMPLE_COLOURS = ("tab:blue", "tab:purple", "tab:red")

found = []
for group in ne.stored_scans(ne.STORE_PATH):

title: Appendix B — Measuring Water:Fat: fitting two Gaussians
text:
To compare the two breasts of a patient, each breast gets one number, its Water:Fat. All of the breast’s scans are peak-shift corrected and min-max normalised (Appendix A), then averaged. A sum of two Gaussians is fitted to that mean curve over q = 7-25 nm⁻¹: one for the fat peak (centre between q = 12 and 16) and one for the broader water peak (centre between q = 17 and 26). The area of each Gaussian within ±3σ of its centre is height × σ × √(2π) × erf(3/√2), and the breast’s Water:Fat is the water Gaussian’s area divided by the fat Gaussian’s area. A breast with more water and less fat has a larger Water:Fat, and comparing the two breasts of one patient removes much of what differs from patient to patient.
Figure B.1 shows this for one patient with one NORMAL and one CANCER breast, each breast the mean of all its scans. Under the water-peak rule the mean is of the breast’s usable scans only (Appendix C).

title: Appendix C — The water-peak rule
text:
C.1 Before and after
The filter that decides whether a scan is usable (water-rich). To be a fair test it must meet three conditions:
Each breast is scanned a few times, usually three, and some of those scans will miss the glandular tissue. So the rule works scan by scan:
This fixed threshold is for single-point Human 1.0 scans, when only a few beams are placed. It is also the natural stopgap on Human 1.0 while mapping is not yet available (Chapter 4): apply the same check during scanning and only keep a position if the short look is water-rich. Chapter 1 (Chapter 1) makes the same “wet = information” point with a top/bottom 15% cut, which is the natural rule once a whole breast is mapped.
Figure C.2 applies the threshold to every breast: rejected (fatty) scans look the same for all three labels; usable scans are wetter for BENIGN and CANCER than for NORMAL, with BENIGN and CANCER almost the same under this cut. The paired comparison that works is CANCER vs NORMAL (Appendix D).
The same paired comparison, one number per patient, using every scan, then only the usable scans, then only the rejected ones:
Using every scan, the CANCER breast is already the wetter one in most patients, but the fatty scans dilute the signal. Taking them out raises the share to 15/18 (83%); the fatty scans on their own are at chance. The rule accepts 39% of all scans. Every patient with both breasts usable under this rule is plotted in Appendix F. Further checks on the threshold and who is left out are in Appendix D.

def signed_differences(min_height, min_centre, rejected=False):
    """{comparison: [first-named − second Water:Fat per patient]}, and {"NORMAL vs NORMAL": [left − right]}."""
    found = rule_breasts(min_height, min_centre, rejected=rejected)
    out = defaultdict(list)
    for nova in sorted({n for n, _ in found if (n, "LEFT") in found and (n, "RIGHT") in found}):

                out[comparison].append(ratio_a - ratio_b)
        if label_a == label_b == "NORMAL":

    return out

D.4 Water peak against age

import h5py
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

# age is stored per scan in the HDF5; one value per Nova
_nova_age = {}
with h5py.File(ne.STORE_PATH, "r") as _store:
    for _group in _store["scans"].values():
        _nova = int(_group.attrs["nova"])
        _age = float(_group.attrs.get("age", np.nan))
        if np.isfinite(_age):

def _age_water_points(label):
    ages, waters = [], []
    for (nova, side, lab), curves in breast_use.items():
        if lab != label or nova not in _nova_age:
            continue
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore", RuntimeWarning)

            water_h = float(np.nanmean(mean_curve[(q >= WATER[0]) & (q <= WATER[1])]))
        if not np.isfinite(water_h):

NoteWhat this means




The rule is, in effect, a breast-density filter. Its scan-by-scan water-peak check, which never sees the clinical records, keeps mostly BI-RADS C/D breasts and drops mostly B. This confirms from independent records that rejected scans come from fatty tissue, not from bad measurements.
This is where it would be most useful. Dense breasts are where mammography is weakest (the reports here repeatedly say density “may obscure small masses”), so a method that works in dense breasts would complement it.
It narrows who the result applies to. The CANCER vs NORMAL result of the rule holds for younger women with dense breasts; for the older, fattier group it currently says nothing.
Age cannot bias the comparison itself: both breasts of a patient have the same age, so age decides only who is compared, not which breast comes out higher.

title: Appendix H — Tumour size by grade
text:
The size of each tumour in our CANCER breasts, by grade, measured two ways. From the pathology reports, the linear extent of invasive tumour measured in the biopsy cores (the largest of a breast’s specimens, lymph node specimens left out); from the radiology reports, the largest mass measured on imaging (mammogram, ultrasound or MRI). The grade is the overall (Nottingham) grade from the pathology reports, taken from the score out of 9 where the report gives one (3-5 grade 1, 6-7 grade 2, 8-9 grade 3) and from the stated grade otherwise. The imaging sizes are taken from the report text and can include more than one mass in a breast, so they are approximate.


Code
GRADES = (1, 2, 3)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # the same horizontal jitter on every render

def plot_by_grade(ax, values, ylabel, title):
    by_grade = {g: [size for grade, size, _ in values if grade == g] for g in GRADES}
    ax.boxplot([by_grade[g] for g in GRADES], positions=range(len(GRADES)), widths=0.5, showfliers=False, patch_artist=True,
               boxprops=dict(facecolor="#d4ebe8", edgecolor="#2a9d8f"), whiskerprops=dict(color="#2a9d8f"), capprops=dict(color="#2a9d8f"),
               medianprops=dict(color="#1d3557", lw=2.2))
    for k, g in enumerate(GRADES):
        for is_usable in (False, True):
            here = [size for grade, size, ok in values if grade == g and ok == is_usable]
            ax.scatter(k + rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18, len(here)), here, s=14 if is_usable else 10, zorder=3,
                       color=TOP_COLOUR if is_usable else "grey", alpha=0.9 if is_usable else 0.5,
                       edgecolor="black" if is_usable else "none", lw=0.4,
                       label=("usable scan" if is_usable else "no usable scan") if k == 0 else None)
    labels = []
    for g in GRADES:
        here = [(size, ok) for grade, size, ok in values if grade == g]
        labels.append(f"Grade {g}\nn={len(here)}\nmean {np.mean([s for s, _ in here]):.1f} mm\n{sum(ok for _, ok in here)} usable"
                      if here else f"Grade {g}\n(n=0)")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(GRADES)), labels)
    ax.set(ylabel=ylabel, title=title, ylim=(0, None))
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")

plot_by_grade(imaging_ax, imaged, "Largest mass on imaging (mm)", "Imaging")

title: Appendix I — Excluding patients with a large left/right intensity imbalance
text:
8 patients with image-total imbalance ≥ 2× excluded; 251 left


A few patients have one breast whose raw images are far brighter than the other (total detector counts), even at similar thickness. That imbalance is rare in Nova 250 onwards (typical left/right ratio near 1) and produces unreliable Water:Fat comparisons — Nova 396 is the example in Figure I.1, where the CANCER side’s mean image total is about 2.4× the NORMAL side’s and the NORMAL curve looks almost fat-free. From here on, a patient is dropped if the brighter breast’s mean image total is at least 2× the dimmer breast’s (breast_image_totals.csv, summed over each Sample Main image before 1D reduction). That removes 8 patients, including Nova 396; 7 of them are among the 258 patients of this analysis, leaving 251.


Code
EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE = 396
exclude_totals = {row.side: float(row.image_total_mean) for row in totals[totals.nova == EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE].itertuples()}
exclude_scans = {}  # side: [(label, curve, water height)]
for side, label, scan_q, curve, _ in ne.read_patients(ne.STORE_PATH, {EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE}, ne.REFERENCES["stretch"])[EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE][0]:
    on_q = np.interp(q, scan_q, curve, left=np.nan, right=np.nan)
    with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
        height = np.nanmean(on_q[(q >= WATER[0]) & (q <= WATER[1])])
    exclude_scans.setdefault(side, []).append((label, on_q, height))

plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4.3), sharey=True)
x = np.linspace(2, 25, 600)
sides = sorted(exclude_scans, key=lambda side: exclude_scans[side][0][0] != "NORMAL")
for ax, side in zip(axes, sides):
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)
    items = exclude_scans[side]
    label = items[0][0]
    curves = [curve for _, curve, _ in items]
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", RuntimeWarning)
        mean = np.nanmean(curves, axis=0)
    p = fit_two_gaussians(mean)
    ratio = water_fat(mean)
    for k, (_, curve, height) in enumerate(items):
        ax.plot(q, curve, color=ne.STATUS_COLOURS[label], lw=0.9, label=f"scan {k + 1}: water {height:.2f}")
    for (height, centre, sigma), colour in ((p[:3], FAT_COLOUR), (p[3:], WATER_COLOUR)):
        within = (x >= centre - 3 * sigma) & (x <= centre + 3 * sigma)
        ax.fill_between(x[within], gaussian(x[within], height, centre, sigma), color=colour, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
    ax.plot(x, two_gaussians(x, *p), color="red", ls="--", lw=1.4, zorder=5, label="fat + water fit")
    img_total = exclude_totals.get(side, np.nan)
    ax.set(title=f"Nova {EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE} {side}, {label}: image total {img_total:.2g}\n"
                  f"Water:Fat = {ratio:.2f}  (patient excluded: imbalance {intensity_ratio[EXCLUDE_EXAMPLE]:.2f}×)",
           xlabel="q (nm⁻¹)", xlim=(2, 25), ylim=(0, 2))
    ax.set_xticks([5, 10, 15, 20, 25])
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
